a: Of David.
t: The last David collection, and how this part is numbered
p: Psalms 138–145 are the last group headed "of David". Hebrew Bibles count some titles as verse 1.
b: Book V closes with eight psalms headed le-david, "of David" (138–145), the last David collection before the five closing "Praise the LORD" psalms (146–150). Many scholars think the editors placed them on purpose, so that David, who leads the prayers of Book I, also leads the last prayers before the final praise (compare 72:20, which says the prayers of David were ended). Numbering: in Hebrew Bibles a title that stands as its own verse is verse 1. In this part that shifts the verse numbers of Psalms 140 and 142, whose titles are separate verses there: 140:1 here is 140:2 in a Hebrew Bible. The Greek and Latin number each of Psalms 138–146 one lower (Psalm 138 is their 137).

a: in front of the gods
p: The Hebrew says elohim, "gods". The Greek has "angels"; the Targum has "judges"; others think of kings.
b: The singer thanks the LORD "in front of the elohim". The word can mean God, gods, or heavenly beings. Readers have taken it four ways: (1) the gods of the nations, whom the singer defies by praising the LORD in their face (compare 96:4–5); (2) the heavenly court, God's council, as in 29:1 and 82:1, which the Greek reads as "angels" (enantion angelōn) and Jerome's Gallican Psalter as in conspectu angelorum; (3) human judges or rulers: the Targum has "judges" (dayyanaya) and Rashi "princes", which fits the kings of 138:4; (4) the gods worshiped by those kings. The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) has the same word, but adds the divine name twice: "I will thank you, LORD, with all my heart", and, written above the line, "in front of the LORD, the gods" (see the variant). The Plain keeps "the gods", as Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew does (deorum).

a: toward your holy temple
p: Bowing toward the temple was the posture of prayer for Israelites away from it, as Solomon's prayer asks.
b: The singer bows "toward" (el) the temple, not inside it. Solomon's prayer asks God to hear those who pray toward the house from far away or from exile (1 Kings 8:29–30, 8:48), and Daniel prays three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). Jews still face Jerusalem to pray. Some scholars think the singer is in the temple courts, facing the inner sanctuary; others, that he is far off. The Greek has the same line, and the Targum and the church fathers sometimes read the temple as heaven, God's true dwelling.

a: for you have made your word great
t: A word greater than his name?
p: The Hebrew seems to say God has made his word great above all his name. Many think the text has slipped.
b: Word for word the line reads "for you have made great, over all your name, your word" (or "your saying", imratekha). Taken as it stands, God has made his promise even greater than everything his name already stood for: what he has now said and done goes beyond his past fame. That is how Rashi and Radak read it, and how the Plain renders it. Others think a word is missing or doubled, and suggest "you have made your name and your word great above all" (an emendation many modern versions follow) or "above all the heavens" (compare 8:1; 57:5). The Greek has "you have made your holy name great over everything", with no "word"; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew has both, super omne nomen tuum eloquium tuum. 11QPs-a agrees with the Hebrew.

a: all the kings of the earth will thank you
p: The rescue of one singer becomes news that the kings of the earth will hear and praise.
b: The psalm moves from one person's answered prayer (138:3) to the kings of the earth. The same hope runs through the royal and Zion psalms (72:10–11; 102:15) and through Isaiah, where kings come to the light of Zion (Isaiah 49:7; 60:3). If the speaker is a king, as the title "of David" suggests to many readers, then other kings are hearing how the LORD kept his word to his king (compare 18:49). The Greek adds a line in 138:1, "for you heard the words of my mouth", which echoes "the words of your mouth" here.

a: he looks on the lowly
p: God is high above all, and that is exactly why he sees the low. The proud he knows only from far off.
b: This is a theme of the whole Bible: the God who lives on high stoops to the lowly (113:5–7; Isaiah 57:15), and the proud keep him at a distance. Hannah sings it (1 Samuel 2:7–8), and Mary's song in Luke takes it up (Luke 1:48–52). "Knows from a distance" can mean he sees through the proud even from far away, or that they never come close to him. The Greek turns it into "he knows the high things from afar".

a: The LORD will carry it through for me
p: The verb gamar means to complete or bring to an end. God will finish what he started for the singer.
b: YHWH yigmor ba'adi is short and bare: "the LORD will complete for me". The object is left out. Most read it as God finishing what he has begun for the singer (compare 57:2, where God "completes" things for the speaker; Philippians 1:6). Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has "LORD, you will repay on my behalf"; Codex Alexandrinus has "he will repay"; both take the verb as settling accounts. The last line, "the works of your hands, do not let them fall", calls the singer himself God's handiwork (compare 139:13–16).

a: LORD, you have probed me, and you know me.
p: The verb chaqar is used for searching out a land or a matter. The psalm opens and closes with it (139:23).
b: Chaqar is the word for spies searching out a land (Judges 18:2) and for judges looking into a case (Deuteronomy 13:14). The psalm opens with it in the past tense, "you have probed me", and closes with it as a request, "Probe me, God" (139:23). In between, the singer learns that being known by God is not only frightening but a wonder (139:6, 14). Whether this is a calm meditation or the prayer of a man under accusation is debated (see the chapter page).

a: You yourself know my sitting down and my getting up
t: Sitting and rising, going and lying down
p: Pairs of opposites mean "everything": all my day, from rest to work, is known to you.
b: Hebrew often names two ends to mean everything between them. Sitting and rising, walking and lying down (139:3), behind and in front (139:5), heaven and Sheol (139:8), darkness and light (139:12) all say the same thing: there is no part of life God does not see. The same pairs describe daily life in the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:7). "From a distance" does not mean God is far away, but that he reads the singer's thoughts before they are spoken, even from heaven (compare 138:6).

a: You sift through my walking and my lying down
p: The verb zarah is used for winnowing grain. God sifts the singer's life as a farmer sifts wheat from chaff.
b: The usual meaning of zarah is to scatter or winnow, tossing grain in the wind to separate it from chaff (Ruth 3:2). The picture is of God sorting through every part of the singer's day. Some take it from a related word for measuring ("you measure my path"); the Greek has "you have tracked out". The Talmud and Rashi also hear winnowing, and apply it to God choosing the best of the seed from which a child is formed (Bavli Niddah 31a). "Familiar" renders hiskanta, to be at home with, used of knowing someone well (Job 22:21).

a: From behind and from the front you close me in
p: The verb tsur can mean to shut in, as in a siege. God's closeness could feel like a guard or like a wall.
b: Tsartani is from tsur, to shut in or besiege (2 Samuel 11:1). Some readers hear threat: the singer cannot get away from God (139:7), as Job felt hemmed in (Job 13:27; 19:8). Others hear protection, a hand laid on the shoulder. The psalm seems to hold both: the wish to flee (139:7–12) turns into wonder (139:14). The rabbis read the verb as yatsar, "to form", and found in it the making of the first human, formed "behind and in front", with two faces (Genesis Rabbah 8:1; Bavli Berakhot 61a).

a: Knowing like this is a wonder beyond me
p: Pil'i (Qere pli'ah), "wonderful", is used for what lies beyond human reach.
b: The word for "wonder" (pele' and its relatives) is used for what only God can do (Exodus 15:11; Isaiah 9:6, Hebrew 9:5). Here it is God's knowledge that is beyond the singer, the way Job admits he spoke of "wonders beyond me" (Job 42:3). The Masoretes read the word with a slightly different spelling (Qere pli'ah); the meaning is the same. The same root returns in 139:14: "I am a wonder... your works are wonders."

a: Where could I go to get away from your spirit?
p: Christian theology calls this God's omnipresence. The psalm states it as experience, not as a doctrine.
b: Christian and Jewish teachers read 139:7–12 as the classic text for God's being present everywhere (later called omnipresence) and knowing everything (139:1–6, omniscience). The psalm does not argue; it imagines running away and finding God already there, like Jonah, who "got up to run away from the LORD's presence" (Jonah 1:3; in Hebrew, from "the face of the LORD") and found him in the sea. "Spirit" (ruach) and "face" are parallel: both mean God's own presence. Christian readers have heard here the Holy Spirit (compare 51:11; 143:10); Jewish readers, God's Presence (the Shekhinah). Jeremiah 23:23–24 asks the same question from God's side.

a: Sheol
p: The world of the dead, under the earth. Even there God is present.
b: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead, pictured below the earth, dark and silent (6:5; 88:3–12). Several psalms say the dead are cut off from God's care (88:5). This verse says the opposite: even if the singer made his bed in Sheol, God would be there. Amos 9:2 uses the same pair, Sheol and heaven, to say no one can escape God's judgment. Here the point is that no one is beyond his reach for good. Christian readers linked the verse to Christ's descent to the dead.

a: Should I take up the wings of the dawn
t: The wings of the dawn and the end of the sea
p: Dawn in the east, the sea in the west: the singer imagines flying from one end of the world to the other.
b: For someone in Israel, dawn rises over the eastern desert and the Mediterranean lies to the west. Flying on the dawn's wings to the far end of the sea means crossing the whole world at the speed of light. In Canaanite poetry Dawn (Shachar) was a god (compare Isaiah 14:12, "son of the dawn"); here the dawn is only a picture. The Greek has "if I take up my wings at dawn" (some copies "straight up").

a: Darkness will surely crush me
p: The Hebrew verb usually means "crush" or "bruise". Many versions emend it to "cover" or "hide".
b: Yeshupheni comes from shuph, the verb the site renders "strike" at Genesis 3:15 and Job 9:17. Read that way, the singer fears the dark will overwhelm him. The Greek agrees, "darkness will trample me" (katapatēsei), and so does the Gallican Latin (conculcabunt), and 11QPs-a has the same consonants. Since "crush" sits oddly beside "the light around me will be night", many scholars change one letter and read yesukkeni, "will cover me", as Jerome did in his Psalter from the Hebrew (operient me). The Greek's second line also differs: "and night is light in my delight". The Plain keeps the Hebrew "crush", which has the support of the Greek, the Gallican Latin and 11QPs-a.

a: dark and light are alike
p: God made both darkness and light, so neither can hide anything from him.
b: In Genesis God names the darkness and the light (Genesis 1:4–5), and Isaiah has God say he forms both (Isaiah 45:7). Job says death and destruction lie open before God (Job 26:6). The New Testament takes the image further: God is light and in him is no darkness (1 John 1:5). In Codex Vaticanus the first two lines of this verse are missing, probably skipped by a copyist; other Greek copies have them.
r: Genesis 1:4–5; Isaiah 45:7; Job 26:6; Job 34:22; Daniel 2:22; 1 John 1:5

a: It was you who made my kidneys
p: Hebrew placed feelings and conscience in the kidneys. The singer means his inmost self.
b: Where English says "heart" for the inner self, Hebrew can say "kidneys" (kilyot), the seat of the deepest feelings and of conscience (16:7; 73:21; Jeremiah 11:20, where God tests "heart and kidneys"). "Made" renders qanita, which can mean create or acquire (Genesis 14:19, 22; Proverbs 8:22). The Targum keeps "kidneys"; the Greek has nephrous, kidneys. Older English "reins" (KJV) is the same image.

a: you wove me together in my mother's womb
p: The same verb pictures God weaving the body in Job 10:11. A child in the womb is God's handiwork.
b: Tesukkeni (from sakhakh or nasakh) means to weave or to shelter. Job uses the same picture: "with bones and sinews you wove me together" (Job 10:11), and asks how God could now destroy what his hands made. Other texts say God formed someone in the womb for a purpose (Jeremiah 1:5; Isaiah 49:1, 5; Galatians 1:15) and that rich and poor alike were made in the womb by the same God (Job 31:15). The Greek reads differently: "you took hold of me from my mother's womb".
r: Job 10:8–12; Job 31:15; Jeremiah 1:5; Isaiah 49:1; Isaiah 44:24; Galatians 1:15

a: embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth
t: Made in the depths of the earth
p: The womb is pictured as the hidden depths of the earth, where the body is embroidered like colored cloth.
b: Ruqqamti is the verb for embroidery or weaving in colors, used for the tabernacle hangings (Exodus 26:36). Veins and sinews were perhaps the threads. "The lowest parts of the earth" is a poetic name for the hidden womb, and it echoes the making of the first human from the ground (Genesis 2:7) and the idea of the earth as everyone's mother (Job 1:21; Sirach 40:1). Job 1:21 puts the two side by side: naked from the mother's womb, naked back "there". Some scholars see an old belief that human beings were first formed inside the earth.

a: Your eyes saw me as a shapeless lump
p: Golmi, "my unformed mass", is the only use of golem in the Bible. Later Jewish lore used the word for a clay man.
b: The noun golem means a rolled-up, unshaped lump, and this is its only appearance in the Bible. It describes the embryo before its parts are shaped. The Talmud uses it for Adam in the first hours of creation, a body without a soul (Bavli Sanhedrin 38b), and medieval legend gave the word to the clay man of Prague. Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has the pronouns swapped, "your unwrought (thing) my eyes saw", but other Greek copies in Swete's apparatus have "my unwrought (thing) your eyes saw", as in the Hebrew; Jerome has informem adhuc me, "me while still unformed". The Targum says "my body".

a: in your scroll all of them were written
t: God's scroll: days, limbs, or a fixed fate?
p: Does "all of them" mean the days of a life or the parts of the body? And are all those days fixed?
b: The Hebrew "all of them" has no clear noun before it. (1) Most modern readers join it to the next line: the days of the singer's life were written in God's book before he lived one of them. (2) The KJV, following some Jewish commentators, supplied "my members": the parts of the body were planned in God's book as they took shape. (3) The Targum makes it all of creation, written on the day the world was made. Readers then differ over what "written" means. Many Reformed teachers cite the verse for God's decree, every day planned. Others, including many Jewish, Arminian and open-theist readers, hear a poet's praise of God's care and knowledge, not a statement that every event is fixed. Compare the book of the living (69:28) and Exodus 32:32–33.

a: how dear your thoughts are
p: Re'eykha usually means "your friends", but here, as in 139:2, "your thoughts". The Greek reads "friends".
b: Rea', "thought", is a rare Aramaic-like word, used in 139:2. Spelled the same way, the word normally means "friend". Rashi read it so: "how dear are your friends", the righteous of every generation. The Greek read "your friends have been greatly honored, God", and the Gallican Latin nimis honorificati sunt amici tui Deus, a line the Western church sang for centuries on the feasts of the apostles, the "friends" of God (compare John 15:15). The Plain follows the sense the context demands: the thoughts of God that the singer cannot count (139:18).
orig: וְלִי מַה־יָּקְרוּ רֵעֶיךָ אֵל (veli mah-yaqru re'eykha 'el)

a: I come awake, and I am with you still
t: Waking up, or reaching the end?
p: Most read heqitsoti as "I wake up". Some read "I come to the end" of counting, and am still with God.
b: Heqitsoti normally means "I awoke" (3:5). Then the singer counts God's thoughts like a man counting sheep, falls asleep, and wakes to find God still with him. A small change of vowels gives haqqitsoti, "I have reached the end" (from qets): even if he finished counting, he would still be in God's presence. Rashi reads it that way. Christian readers since the early church heard a hint of resurrection: "I arose, and I am still with you" (Greek exēgerthēn), and the Roman Mass of Easter Day opens with this verse in Latin, Resurrexi et adhuc tecum sum.

a: God, if only you would put the wicked to death!
t: The sudden turn to the wicked
p: After the wonder of 139:1–18 the psalm turns to the wicked. Some lectionaries leave 139:19–22 out.
b: The turn is abrupt, and many readers find it jarring. Several explanations are given. (1) The singer has been accused by "bloodstained men" and the whole psalm is his plea of innocence before the God who knows him (compare 17:3; Job 31). (2) Being so close to God, he cannot stand beside those who hate God, and says so in the strongest words he has (139:21–22). (3) The lines are a later addition. In worship the verses are often skipped: the Roman Liturgy of the Hours since 1971 omits 139:19–22, and the Revised Common Lectionary appoints 139:1–6, 13–18 or 139:1–12, 23–24, never 19–22. See the curse psalms topic.

a: your enemies take it up for something empty
t: Taking God's name up for nothing
p: The words echo the third commandment: "You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty."
b: Nasu lashav, "they take up for emptiness", is the language of Exodus 20:7, "You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty." The object "your name" is not written here, but readers since the Targum ("they swear by your name falsely") have supplied it. The word for "enemies", 'arekha, is unusual (it is the Aramaic word; in Hebrew the same letters mean "your cities"). The Greek took it as "cities": "they will take your cities in vain". "Talk of you" in the first line may also be read "rebel against you", with a small change of letters.

a: I hate them with a hatred that holds nothing back
p: The phrase tachlit sin'ah, "completeness of hatred", is famous as "perfect hatred" in older English.
b: The KJV's "perfect hatred" made the line famous. Jewish and Christian readers have explained it in several ways. Augustine taught that a "perfect hatred" hates the sin in a person and loves the person, so it can sit beside love of enemies (City of God 14.6; Expositions on this psalm). Others read it as loyalty: a servant cannot be friends with his master's enemies (compare 2 Chronicles 19:2). C. S. Lewis judged such lines dangerous to imitate but honest. Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:43–44) is the background every Christian reader brings. The singer turns at once from hating others to asking God to search him (139:23–24).

a: a hurtful way
t: A way of pain, or a way of idols?
p: Derekh 'otsev can mean a painful or harmful way, or, with another meaning of the same letters, "a way of idols".
b: The noun 'otsev usually means pain or hurt (Isaiah 14:3), and a related word means idol (Isaiah 48:5). So the singer may ask God to see whether there is "a way that hurts" (others, or himself) in him, or "a way of idolatry". Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, chose idols (via idoli); the Greek has "a way of lawlessness"; the Targum "a way of those who stray". The Plain keeps the more common sense, with this note.

a: lead me along the everlasting road
t: The everlasting road, or the ancient road?
p: Derekh 'olam can mean the road that lasts forever or the road of long ago, the old paths of faithfulness.
b: 'Olam means a very long time, past or future. Jeremiah speaks of the "paths of long ago" where the good way is (Jeremiah 6:16; 18:15), and some read the line as a prayer to be led in that old way of Israel's faith. Others hear the way that leads to lasting life, in contrast to the way of the wicked that perishes (1:6). The Greek and Latin have "the eternal way" (hodō aiōnia, via aeterna).

a: For the music director
p: Psalm 140 is the last of the fifty-five psalms headed lamnatseach, "for the music director".
b: The heading lamnatseach stands over fifty-five psalms, and this is the last; the meaning is debated (see 4:0). The Greek renders it "for the end" (eis to telos), which church fathers read as pointing to Christ, the end of the law. Psalms 140–143 are a small group of laments of David, each asking to be rescued from enemies who set traps (140:5; 141:9; 142:3; 143:9).

a: under their lips lies the venom of the viper
p: Paul quotes this line from the Greek in his chain of verses showing that all have sinned.
b: In Romans 3:10–18 Paul strings together lines from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that Jews and Gentiles alike are "under sin". Romans 3:13 joins 5:9 ("their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they deceive") to this verse in the Greek wording, "the venom of asps is under their lips". The snake image fits slander: words that strike unseen and poison (58:4; James 3:8). The animal ('akhshuv, found only here) is unknown; Rashi says a spider, and the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) has 'akkavish, the ordinary Hebrew word for spider. The Greek and the Targum have a snake.

a: Selah
p: A word of unknown meaning, probably a musical or liturgical mark. This is its last use but one in the Psalms.
b: Selah appears seventy-one times in the Psalms, often at the end of a section. No one knows what it meant: perhaps "lift up" (a louder passage, or a raising of the voice), a pause, or a point for a refrain or a bow. The Greek has diapsalma, "interlude". Psalm 140 has it three times (140:3, 5, 8), and its last use in the Psalter is 143:6.

a: they have laid out ropes as a net by the trail
p: The pictures come from bird hunting: hidden traps, a net pulled by a cord, and baited snares.
b: Ancient hunters caught birds with clap nets: a net spread on the ground beside a path, a long cord to pull it shut, and bait or a spring trap (moqesh) to catch a foot. Egyptian tomb paintings show such nets. The psalmists use the same scene for plotters who set legal or social traps for the innocent (91:3; 124:7; 141:9; 142:3). Rashi explains the cord tied to the net that the hunter pulls when the birds settle.

a: LORD, my Lord
p: The order here is the divine name first, then "my Lord". It is not the usual "Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH).
b: Usually the two names stand as Adonai YHWH, "the Lord GOD" (71:5). Here, and in 68:20, 109:21, 141:8 and Habakkuk 3:19, the order is reversed, YHWH Adonai. The Plain gives "LORD, my Lord" here, as at 109:21, and "the LORD, the Lord" at 68:20. The Greek has "Lord, Lord" (Kyrie kyrie). "My strong salvation" is literally "strength of my salvation". "The day the weapons clash" is "the day of weaponry", the day of battle; God covers the head like a helmet (compare Ephesians 6:17).

a: or they will hold themselves high
p: The last word of 140:8, yarumu, "they rise high", may belong to 140:9: "they raise the heads of those who surround me".
b: The Masoretic division ends 140:8 with yarumu selah, "they will be lifted high. Selah", and starts 140:9 with "the heads of those who surround me". Many scholars move the word down: "those who surround me raise their heads" (a gesture of pride, 83:2), "may the harm of their lips cover them". The Greek kept the Masoretic division ("lest they be exalted. Interlude"). The Plain follows the Hebrew verse division. Rashi reads "scheme" (zemamo) as a muzzle, following an old midrash: do not let the wicked off his bit.

a: Let hot coals rain down on them
p: The curse asks for the punishment of Sodom: fire from above and pits below. Proverbs and Paul use coals differently.
b: The images recall the judgment on Sodom (Genesis 19:24; compare Psalm 11:6, "fiery coals and sulfur") and the earth opening under Korah (Numbers 16:31–33). Mahamorot, "deep holes", appears only here; Rashi takes it from a word for rebellion. As in all the curse psalms, the singer hands vengeance to God ("let him make them fall"); he does not take it himself. The same picture is turned around in Proverbs 25:21–22, which Paul quotes in Romans 12:20: feed your enemy, and you heap burning coals on his head.

a: the man with the slandering tongue
p: Ish lashon, "a man of tongue", means a slanderer, one whose words do the damage.
b: "A man of tongue" is a Hebrew way to say a slanderer or a man who wins by talk (compare Sirach 8:3; "the master of the tongue" in Ecclesiastes 10:11). The psalm's enemies attack with words: sharpened tongues (140:3), the harm of their lips (140:9). Later Jewish teaching on lashon hara, "evil speech", gathers verses like these. "Thrust after thrust" renders lemadchephot, "for blows" or "for overthrow", a word found only here.

a: the LORD will plead the case of the poor
t: God takes the poor man's case
p: The singer ends by trusting that God acts as lawyer and judge for the poor and needy.
b: Din is a court case, and mishpat the rights or justice due to someone. The LORD is the one who argues the poor man's case and wins his rights (9:4; 82:3; Proverbs 22:22–23; Jeremiah 22:16). Whether the speaker is a king or not, he puts himself among the poor (compare 40:17; 86:1). The psalm ends, like many laments, with the righteous giving thanks in God's presence (140:13; compare 11:7).

a: Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you
p: Incense was burned morning and evening in the temple. The singer asks that his prayer count as that offering.
b: Aaron was to burn incense on the golden altar every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7–8), and its rising smoke became a picture of prayer going up to God. Luke has the people praying outside while Zechariah burns the incense (Luke 1:10), and in Revelation the incense in golden bowls "are the prayers of God's people" (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4). Whether the singer is far from the temple and offers prayer instead of incense, or prays at the temple at the hour of the offering, is debated.

a: the evening grain offering
p: Minchat 'erev is the grain offering that went with the evening sacrifice, the hour of prayer in later books.
b: Minchah is the site's "grain offering" (terms), the offering of flour and oil (Leviticus 2). The daily evening lamb was offered with a grain offering (Exodus 29:38–41), and "the time of the evening grain offering" became a set hour of prayer: Elijah prays at it (1 Kings 18:36), and so do Ezra (Ezra 9:4–5) and Daniel (Daniel 9:21). The Greek has "evening sacrifice" (thysia hesperinē). This verse is the reason Psalm 141 became the evening psalm of the church (see the chapter page).

a: post a guard for my mouth
p: Before asking to be kept from evil men, the singer asks to be kept from his own words.
b: The door of the lips is a picture of control over speech (Micah 7:5). The singer's first fear is not the enemy's tongue (140:3) but his own. Proverbs says the one who guards his mouth guards his life (Proverbs 13:3; 21:23), and Sirach turns this verse into a prayer: "Who will set a guard over my mouth?" (Sirach 22:27). James 3:2–12 makes the same point. Rashi reads it as a prayer to speak rightly when praying.

a: Let me not taste their dainty food
t: Refusing the table of the wicked
p: To eat with someone was to share his life. The singer will not join the feasts of those who do wrong.
b: Meals sealed friendship and covenant (Genesis 31:54). Refusing "their dainty food" means refusing to be drawn into the circle of evildoers and their profits (compare 1:1; Proverbs 23:1–3, 6–8). Daniel refused the king's food for a similar reason (Daniel 1:8). The Greek made the line about speech: "do not turn my heart to evil words, to make excuses for sins", and the Latin ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis was long used in Western prayers of confession.

a: If a righteous man hits me, it is loyal love
t: A hard verse: the blows of a friend
p: Being corrected by a good man is a kindness, like oil on the head. The Hebrew of 141:5–7 is very difficult.
b: Most read 141:5 as the other side of 141:4: the singer would rather be struck and scolded by a righteous man, which is loyal love (hesed), than feast with the wicked (compare Proverbs 27:6, "Wounds from someone who loves you are true"; Proverbs 9:8). Oil on the head was a sign of welcome and joy (23:5). Rashi takes the righteous man as a prophet like Nathan, and the oil as David's royal anointing, which should not make him too proud to accept correction. The last line is unclear: "my prayer is still against their evil deeds" is the usual reading; others read "in their misfortunes", that is, the singer will still pray for them. Verses 5–7 have more proposed emendations than almost any other lines in the Psalms.

a: Their judges are flung down the face of the cliff
p: The Hebrew says their judges were released "into the hands of the rock". It may describe an execution or a defeat.
b: Nishmetu vide-sela' shofteyhem is obscure. Many read it as the leaders of the wicked being thrown down a cliff, a known way of executing (2 Chronicles 25:12; Luke 4:29). Then "they will hear my words, how pleasant they are" means the followers will listen once their leaders fall. Rashi reads the "rock" as the stony heart that leads judges astray. Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has "their powerful ones were swallowed up beside a rock"; other Greek copies in Swete's apparatus have "their judges", as the Hebrew does, and so does the Gallican Latin (iudices). Some church fathers read the rock as Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). No reading is sure, and the Plain stays close to the words.

a: so our bones have been strewn at the mouth of Sheol
t: Our bones, my bones, their bones
p: The image is a plowed field: bones scattered like clods at the edge of the grave.
b: The simile is a farmer breaking up the soil and leaving clods everywhere; so bones lie scattered at the edge of the grave, unburied. Whose bones? The witnesses differ ("our", "my", "their"); the variant on this line gives them. The Plain keeps the Masoretic "our". For Sheol, see 139:8.
orig: נִפְזְרוּ עֲצָמֵינוּ לְפִי שְׁאוֹל (nifzeru 'atsameinu lefi she'ol)

a: do not empty out my life
t: Do not pour out my life
p: The verb 'arah means to pour out or empty, as Rebekah emptied her jar. Isaiah 53:12 uses it of the servant.
b: Al te'ar nafshi uses the verb of Genesis 24:20, where Rebekah empties her jar into the trough, and of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant "poured out his life to death". The singer asks not to be drained like water poured on the ground (compare 22:14; 2 Samuel 14:14). The Greek has "do not take away my life". "I take shelter in you" is the trust formula of the Psalms (2:12; 7:1; 16:1).

a: Let the wicked drop into their own nets
p: The trap-setters fall into their own nets, a frequent hope in the Psalms and Proverbs.
b: The idea that evil recoils on those who plan it runs through the wisdom books and the Psalms (7:15–16; 9:15; 35:8; 57:6; Proverbs 26:27; 28:10). The story of Haman, hanged on his own pole, is its narrative form (Esther 7:10). "All of them at once" renders yachad, "together"; the Greek read it with the last line: "I am alone until I pass by".

a: when he was in the cave
p: David hid in the cave of Adullam and in a cave at En-gedi. Rashi chooses En-gedi, where he cut Saul's robe.
b: Two caves appear in David's story: Adullam, where his family and the desperate gathered to him (1 Samuel 22:1–2), and the cave near En-gedi, where Saul came in and David cut off the corner of his robe (1 Samuel 24:1–7). Psalm 57's title also mentions "the cave". Rashi links Psalm 142 to En-gedi; others to Adullam, where David was alone, then surrounded (142:7; 1 Samuel 22:2). Most critical scholars think the title was added later by readers who matched the psalm's "prison" (142:7) to David's hiding place. This is the last psalm titled maskil, a word of uncertain meaning (see 32:0).

a: Look to my right side and see
t: No one at my right hand
p: In court a defender stood at the right of the accused. The singer looks there and finds no one.
b: The right side was the place of a protector or advocate (16:8; 109:31; 110:5; 121:5). The singer looks to his right and finds no one who "knows" him, that is, no one who will stand up for him. The verb can be read as "look" (addressed to God) or as "I look". The Greek has "I was looking to the right". "No one asks after my life" is literally "no one seeks for my soul": no one cares whether I live.

a: my allotted share in the land of the living
p: Cheleq, "share, portion", is the word for a family's plot of land. The singer has God himself as his share.
b: When Canaan was divided, each family received its cheleq, its share of land. The Levites got no land: "I am your share", God told Aaron (Numbers 18:20). The psalms take up the image for any faithful person: the LORD is the singer's share (16:5; 73:26; 119:57; Lamentations 3:24). Here the hunted man who has lost every place to run (142:4) claims God as his share "in the land of the living", in this life, not only after death (27:13).

a: Lead me out of the prison
t: A real prison, or the cave?
p: The "prison" may be the cave, a real jail, or deep trouble. Francis of Assisi is said to have died praying this psalm.
b: Readers who follow the title take the prison to be the cave where David hid (142:0). Others think the speaker was really jailed, perhaps a debtor or an accused man (compare 107:10–16), or that "prison" is a picture of distress, as "Sheol" often is. The Targum and many Christian readers took it as the soul held in the body or in sin, and the early lives of Francis of Assisi (died 1226) report that he sang this psalm (Greek and Latin 141, Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi) as he was dying. "The righteous will crowd around me" could also be read "will crown me" (yakhtiru, from keter, crown); Rashi reads "the righteous will crown you", and the Greek "the righteous will wait for me".

a: A psalm of David.
p: The church counts Psalm 143 as the seventh and last of the Penitential Psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).
b: From at least the time of Cassiodorus (about 540), Western Christians grouped seven psalms of repentance: 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. They were prayed in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, set to music by composers such as Orlande de Lassus, and Luther published a commentary on them (1517). Psalm 143 earns its place by 143:2: no one is in the right before God. The Greek title, in Codex Vaticanus and the Gallican Latin (quando filius eum persequebatur), adds "when his son was pursuing him", tying it to Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15–17; compare Psalm 3:0). Rashi says it was prayed by all Israel in Babylon.

a: Answer me by your faithfulness, by your righteousness.
p: The singer appeals to God's righteousness, not as a threat but as the reason God will save him.
b: In the Psalms God's "righteousness" (tsedaqah) is often his faithful action to set things right for those who trust him, so it stands beside faithfulness, loyal love and salvation (31:1; 71:2; 143:11). The singer asks God to answer "by your righteousness" in the very breath before he admits that he himself cannot stand in God's court (143:2). Luther said that learning to read "the righteousness of God" in this way, as God's gift to the sinner and not only as his justice against him, changed his life; the Psalms and Romans 1:17 were the texts he worked on.

a: for no living person is in the right in your presence
t: No one is in the right: Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16
p: Paul echoes this line twice: no flesh will be put in the right before God by works of the law.
b: Paul's words in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16, that "no flesh will be put in the right" before God "by works of the law", follow the Greek of this verse (ou dikaiōthēsetai enōpion sou pas zōn) closely, adding "by works of the law" and saying "flesh" for "living person". The same conviction runs through Job (Job 4:17; 9:2; 25:4) and Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:46). The singer does not claim innocence, as some psalmists do (17:3; 26:1); he asks God not to bring the case to trial at all. Luther counted this psalm among his "Pauline psalms" with 32, 51 and 130.
r: Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16; Job 4:17; Job 9:2; Job 25:4; 1 Kings 8:46; 130:3; Ecclesiastes 7:20

a: like the dead of long ago
p: "He has put me in dark places like the dead of long ago": Lamentations 3:6 has the same words, two of them reversed.
b: Lamentations 3:6 has the same words with the first two reversed, bemachashakkim hoshivani kemetei 'olam; here it is hoshivani vemachashakkim. One text borrowed from the other, or both drew on a stock line of lament. Rashi's comment that Israel in Babylon prayed this psalm fits the link with Lamentations, the laments over the fall of Jerusalem. "The dead of long ago" are those long buried and forgotten, the opposite of the "days from long ago" the singer remembers in 143:5, when God acted.

a: my soul reaches for you like weary land
p: Hands spread in prayer and a soul like parched land: the posture and the need.
b: Spreading the hands, palms up, was the gesture of prayer (28:2; 1 Kings 8:22; Exodus 9:29). The singer's whole self (nefesh, throat, life, soul) is like ground cracked by drought, waiting for rain (63:1; Isaiah 44:3). This Selah is the last in the Psalter (see 140:3).

a: I have hidden myself in you
p: The Hebrew kissiti, "I have covered", is odd. The Greek has "I fled to you"; many emend to "I take shelter".
b: Read as it stands, elekha khissiti means "to you I have covered" or "I have hidden (myself) with you". Rashi explains: I hide my troubles from everyone else and tell them to you. The Greek has "I fled for refuge to you" (katephygon, see the variant), which may reflect a different Hebrew, and many scholars read chasiti, "I take shelter", the usual phrase (7:1; 141:8). Jerome from the Hebrew has "I was protected by you". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: May your spirit, which is good, guide me
p: Nehemiah 9:20 also speaks of God's "good spirit". Codex Vaticanus has "holy spirit"; the Targum has both.
b: God's "good spirit" appears again in Nehemiah 9:20, where it instructed Israel in the wilderness. Here it guides the singer on level ground, a life without stumbling (27:11; Isaiah 26:7). Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has "your holy spirit" (to pneuma sou to hagion) and "in the level (way)"; other Greek copies in Swete's apparatus have "your good spirit" (to agathon) and "in a level land", as does the Gallican Latin (spiritus tuus bonus). The Targum combines both: "your holy spirit, the good one" (ruach qudshakh tava). Christian readers heard the Holy Spirit who leads God's children (Romans 8:14; Galatians 5:18); Jewish readers, God's guidance through the Torah ("teach me to do your will").

a: for I am your servant
t: A prayer for the enemies' end
p: The penitent who asked for mercy ends by asking God to destroy his enemies. Readers have found this hard.
b: The psalm that confesses no one is righteous (143:2) ends by asking God to "silence" and destroy the enemies. Some readers see a contradiction; others say the singer asks God, not himself, to deal with those who are crushing his life (143:3), on the basis of God's loyal love for his servant. "Your servant" frames the psalm (143:2, 12): the one who belongs to God asks his master to protect him. See the curse psalms topic.

a: Of David.
p: The Greek title reads "Of David. Against Goliath." 144:10 mentions David freed from "the deadly sword".
b: The Hebrew title has only "of David". The Greek adds "against Goliath" (pros ton Goliad; the Gallican Latin adversus Goliad), probably because the psalm speaks of hands trained for battle (144:1) and of David rescued "from the deadly sword" (144:10; compare 1 Samuel 17:45–51, where David kills Goliath with his own sword). Psalm 151, which follows the Psalter in the Greek, also tells of Goliath. Rashi links 144:10 instead to the day Saul was called away from David (1 Samuel 23:26–28).

a: who teaches my hands to fight a war
p: 144:1–11 reuses lines of Psalm 18, David's song of victory, in a new order.
b: Almost every line of 144:1–11 has a partner in Psalm 18 (and 2 Samuel 22): "blessed is my rock" (18:46), "he teaches my hands to fight" (18:34), "my fortress... the one who gets me free... my shield" (18:2), "who brings nations down beneath me" (18:47), "he bent the sky low and came down" (18:9), lightning and arrows (18:14), the hand from on high and the great waters (18:16), and the sons of foreign lands (18:44–45). What Psalm 18 tells as a past rescue, Psalm 144 asks for again. Many scholars think a later king, or the community after the exile, prayed David's song anew. The Plain uses the site's Psalm 18 wording where the Hebrew is the same.

a: my loyal love
p: The singer calls God himself "my hesed". Some suggest a scribal slip for "my strength".
b: Calling God "my loyal love" (chasdi) is bold: the one who shows loyal love is named by it (compare 59:10, 17, "my God of loyal love"; Jonah 2:8). Some scholars think a letter has dropped and read "my strength" or "my rock", to match the list of strongholds. The Greek has "my mercy" (eleos mou), and 11QPs-a agrees with the Hebrew. The Plain keeps it.

a: what is a human being, that you know him
p: The question of 8:4 returns, but here it leads to a different answer: humans are a puff of air.
b: Psalm 8:4 asks "what is a mere mortal, that you remember him?" and answers with wonder at the honor God gives humans. Job turns the question bitter: "What is a mortal, that you treat him as so great?" (Job 7:17), meaning, why does God not leave him alone? Here the question leads to frailty: a human is a breath, a passing shadow (144:4), and yet the king asks that very God to come down and fight for him. Hebrews 2:6–9 reads the Psalm 8 form of the question of Jesus.

a: A human is like a puff of air
p: Hevel, a breath or vapor, is the keyword of Ecclesiastes, and the name of Abel.
b: Hevel means breath, the mist of breath on a cold day. It is the word Ecclesiastes repeats ("vapor of vapors", Ecclesiastes 1:2), and the name of Abel, whose life was short (Genesis 4:2). Psalm 39:5 and 62:9 use it of human life. "A shadow that slips past" recalls 102:11 and 109:23, and Job 14:2. Rashi explains: Solomon called life a shadow (Ecclesiastes 6:12) without saying which kind, the lasting shadow of a wall or a palm tree; his father David had already said "a passing shadow", the shadow of a bird in flight.

a: whose right hand is a right hand that lies
p: People raised the right hand to swear. A "right hand of falsehood" means a false oath or a broken treaty.
b: Raising the right hand was the gesture of an oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40; Isaiah 62:8), and giving the right hand sealed an agreement (Ezra 10:19). Foreigners whose right hand "lies" are those who break treaties and swear falsely. Rashi draws the contrast: their mouth speaks emptiness, and their oath hand swears falsely.

a: a new song I will sing you
p: A "new song" answers a new act of God. The phrase runs from the Psalms to Revelation.
b: The call to sing a "new song" appears in 33:3, 40:3, 96:1, 98:1 and 149:1, and in Isaiah 42:10. It usually follows a fresh victory or rescue. Revelation has the elders and the 144,000 sing "a new song" to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9; 14:3). The ten-string harp appears also in 33:2 and 92:3.

a: Then our sons will be like young plants
p: In the Hebrew, 144:12–14 pictures Israel's blessings. In the Greek and Latin it describes the foreigners' wealth.
b: The last verses change style and may be a separate blessing joined to the psalm. They begin with asher, "which" or "so that", and most read them as Israel's hope once God rescues the king: healthy children, full barns, safe walls. The Greek read the pronouns as "their" ("whose sons are like young plants... their daughters adorned like a temple"), so that the lines describe the rich foreigners of 144:11, and then 144:15 says: "They called happy the people who have these things; happy is the people whose God is the LORD." Augustine and other Latin fathers preached it that way, as a warning against envying the prosperity of the wicked. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: our daughters like corner columns
p: Zaviyyot are corners or corner pieces. Daughters are pictured as carved pillars, tall and fine.
b: Zaviyyot are corners, as of the altar (Zechariah 9:15). The picture may be of carved corner pillars of a palace, like the women-shaped columns of some ancient buildings, or simply of the solid, handsome stonework at the corners of a fine house. Rashi pictures tall, straight daughters like well-matched cornerstones. The point is strength and beauty, the next generation as a palace still being built.

a: There will be no breach and no going out
p: This may mean no breach in the walls and no exile, or no miscarriage among the cattle.
b: Ein perets ve'ein yotset is short and unclear. (1) Military: no breach in the city wall and no one led out as a captive (compare Amos 4:3, "you will go out through the breaches"), which suits "no cry of grief in our squares". (2) Farming: the cattle "loaded" with young will have no miscarriage (perets as a breaking out, yotset as a calf born dead), which suits the herds of 144:13–14a. Rashi reads the first line as leaders "carried" by their people, and "no going out" as no bad news spreading. The Plain keeps the bare words.

a: Happy is the people whose God is the LORD!
p: This verse, with 84:4, opens the Jewish prayer Ashrei, which leads into Psalm 145.
b: In the Jewish prayer book, Psalm 145 is not said alone. It is introduced by two verses that begin with ashrei, "happy": 84:4 ("Happy are the ones who live in your house") and this verse; then the whole of Psalm 145 follows, and 115:18 closes it. The prayer is called Ashrei from its first word. See 145:0. For "Happy" (ashrei), see 1:1; 33:12 has nearly the same line.

a: A praise of David.
p: Tehillah, "praise", heads only this psalm, yet its plural, Tehillim, became the Hebrew name of the whole book.
b: Many psalms are called mizmor ("a psalm") or shir ("a song"); only Psalm 145 is called tehillah, "a praise". Its plural, Tehillim, "Praises", is the Hebrew name of the book of Psalms. The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) heads it instead tefillah le-david, "A prayer of David" (see the variant). The Greek has ainesis, "praise".

a: I will raise you high, my God, the King
p: Psalm 145 is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, but the nun verse is missing.
b: Each verse opens with the next of the twenty-two Hebrew letters: 1 alef, 2 bet, 3 gimel, 4 dalet, 5 he, 6 waw, 7 zayin, 8 chet, 9 tet, 10 yod, 11 kaf, 12 lamed, 13 mem, (nun missing in the Masoretic Text), 14 samekh, 15 ayin, 16 pe, 17 tsade, 18 qof, 19 resh, 20 shin, 21 tav. The alphabet says that God is praised "from A to Z", fully, and it made the psalm easy to memorize. For the missing nun line see 145:13. Other alphabet psalms are 9–10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112 and 119.

a: my God, the King
p: The psalm names God "the King" and praises his kingdom (145:11–13). Book V ends by crowning God as king.
b: In the Psalter's last David psalm, David himself calls God "my God, the King". Many scholars read this as the editors' answer to the loss of David's line (89:38–51): the human king bows to the true King, whose kingdom lasts forever (145:13; compare 93:1; 146:10; 149:2). Jesus' preaching of "the kingdom of God" draws on this language, and the doxology some manuscripts add to the Lord's Prayer, "yours is the kingdom", echoes 1 Chronicles 29:11.

a: The LORD is great, and much to be praised
p: The first line repeats 48:1 and 96:4. "No searching out" echoes Job and Isaiah 40:28.
b: Gadol YHWH umehullal me'od stands in 48:1 and 96:4 (and 1 Chronicles 16:25). "There is no searching out his greatness" uses the word cheqer, from the verb of 139:1, "probed": God has searched the singer through, but no one can search God through (Job 5:9; 9:10; 11:7; Isaiah 40:28). Paul sings the same in Romans 11:33.

a: Each generation will praise your works to the next
p: Praise is passed from parents to children: one generation tells the next what God has done.
b: Telling the next generation is a duty in Israel (78:4–7; Deuteronomy 6:20–25; Exodus 12:26–27). The verbs move between "they" and "I" (145:4–7): the singer joins a long line of people who speak of God's deeds. Rashi notes this: generation to generation will praise, "and I too" will speak.

a: Gracious and compassionate is the LORD
p: The line repeats God's self-description to Moses, the most quoted creed in the Hebrew Bible.
b: When God passed before Moses he proclaimed himself "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). This sentence is repeated across the Bible: 86:15; 103:8; 111:4; Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2. Here the order is "gracious and compassionate", as in Joel, Jonah, 111:4 and 112:4. Jonah complains that this is exactly why he ran away: God would forgive Nineveh. Psalm 145 goes further than Exodus 34 in one way: the LORD's compassion rests on "all his works" (145:9).

a: The LORD is good to everyone
p: God's goodness reaches every creature, not only Israel. Jews and Christians have read the verse widely.
b: Tov YHWH lakkol: the LORD is good to all, and his compassion is on all his works. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Judah the Prince was spared further suffering after he stopped his servant from sweeping away young weasels, quoting this verse (Bavli Bava Metzia 85a): God's mercy reaches animals too. Jesus says the Father sends sun and rain on good and evil alike (Matthew 5:45), and Paul tells the people of Lystra that God "did good" to the nations by giving rain and harvests (Acts 14:17). Some Christians cite the verse for God's love for all people; others distinguish this general goodness from saving grace (the "common grace" of Reformed theology).

a: They will tell of your kingdom's glory
t: Claude's theory: the king verses and the missing nun
p: Verses 11–13 begin with kaf, lamed and mem, which read backward spell melekh, "king", as commentators often note.
b: The three verses about God's kingdom (145:11–13) begin with the letters kaf, lamed and mem, which read in reverse give m-l-k, melekh, "king". This is a well-known observation in commentary on Psalm 145, not a new one. Claude's own guess builds on it: if the poet shaped the center of the alphabet around the word "king", he would hardly have broken the alphabet in the very next line, so the missing nun line (145:13) is more likely to have been lost or left out later than never written. This is a guess, not evidence; the variant on 145:13 gives the case on both sides.

a: to make his mighty deeds known to human beings
p: The Hebrew switches from "your" to "his" in this verse. The Greek, in Vaticanus and the Gallican Latin, has "your".
b: Verses 10–11 speak to God ("your kingdom"), but 145:12 speaks about him ("his mighty deeds... his kingdom"), and then 145:13 turns back to "your kingdom". Codex Vaticanus (Swete), the Gallican Latin and many modern versions make it "your" throughout (see the variant). The shift may show the singer turning to the listening "human beings" as he speaks. The Plain keeps the Hebrew "his", as Jerome did from the Hebrew (fortitudines eius).

a: Your kingdom is a kingdom for all ages
p: The line returns in Aramaic in Daniel, on the lips of a pagan king.
b: Nebuchadnezzar, humbled, praises the Most High in almost the same words: "his kingdom is a kingdom that lasts forever, and his rule is from generation to generation" (Daniel 4:3; 4:34, in Aramaic). The Targum of this verse is close to Daniel's wording. In the New Testament, Christ's kingdom "will have no end" (Luke 1:33), and the eternal King is praised in 1 Timothy 1:17.
r: Daniel 4:3; Daniel 4:34; Daniel 7:14; Luke 1:33; 1 Timothy 1:17; Exodus 15:18

a: God is faithful in his words and loyal in all his works.
p: The Masoretic Text has no verse for nun. A Qumran scroll and the Greek have one, and the Plain prints it.
b: Between the mem verse (145:13) and the samekh verse (145:14), the Leningrad Codex and most medieval Hebrew manuscripts have nothing: the alphabet skips nun. The Talmud explains why: nun begins Amos 5:2, "She has fallen, and she will not rise again, the virgin Israel" (the first Hebrew word is naflah, "has fallen"), so David left it out, and in the next line he gave support to the fallen (Bavli Berakhot 4b; Rashi). The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) reads ne'eman 'elohim bidvarav vechasid bekhol ma'asav, "God is faithful in his words and loyal in all his works". The Greek has it (with "the Lord" and "holy"), and BHS reports it in one medieval Hebrew manuscript, Kennicott 142, and in the Syriac. The variant weighs the evidence.
orig: נֶאֱמָן אֱלֹהִים בִּדְבָרָיו וְחָסִיד בְּכָל־מַעֲשָׂיו (ne'eman 'elohim bidvarav vechasid bekhol ma'asav), 11QPs-a

a: The LORD gives support to all who are falling
p: God holds up those who stumble and straightens those bent over. The rabbis read it as the answer to Amos 5:2.
b: The verse speaks of all who are falling and all who are bent double, under burdens, illness or shame (compare 146:8; Luke 13:11–13, the woman bent double). In Jewish prayer the morning blessing "who straightens those who are bent" (zoqef kefufim) takes its words from 146:8; compare here, zoqef lekhol hakkefufim. The rabbis heard the verse as God's reply to Amos's cry that Israel had fallen and would not rise (Amos 5:2; Bavli Berakhot 4b). In the West (that is, in the land of Israel), the Talmud adds, people read Amos's words differently: "She has fallen and will fall no more; rise, virgin Israel!"

a: You open your hand
p: Jews and Christians both pray 145:15–16 at meals. The Talmud calls 145:16 the reason the psalm is said daily.
b: The Talmud teaches that whoever says Psalm 145 three times a day may be sure of a share in the world to come, because it is an alphabet poem and because it contains "You open your hand" (Bavli Berakhot 4b). Jewish law asks for special attention at this verse when Ashrei is said. Christians took 145:15–16 as a table prayer: Benedictine monks said Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine ("The eyes of all hope in you, Lord") before meals, and Luther's Small Catechism (1529) teaches children to say these two verses as grace. "What it longs for" renders ratson, "favor, good pleasure"; it can mean either the creature's desire or God's goodwill that satisfies it.

a: Near is the LORD to everyone who calls to him
p: The nearness of God to those who call on him echoes Deuteronomy 4:7. James and Paul take it up.
b: Moses asks what great nation has a god so near as the LORD is whenever Israel calls (Deuteronomy 4:7). The psalm opens that nearness to "everyone" who calls "truly" (be'emet), that is, sincerely and faithfully (Isaiah 55:6; Jeremiah 29:13). James 4:8 ("Come near to God, and he will come near to you") and Paul at Athens (Acts 17:27) say the same.
r: Deuteronomy 4:7; 34:18; Isaiah 55:6; Jeremiah 29:13; James 4:8; Acts 17:27; Philippians 4:5

a: let every creature of flesh bless his holy name
p: The last line widens praise from "my mouth" to "all flesh", preparing for 150:6.
b: "All flesh" (kol basar) means every living creature, often humans but sometimes animals too (Genesis 6:12–13; Isaiah 40:5–6; Joel 2:28). The singer begins alone ("I will raise you high", 145:1) and ends calling on every creature. Psalms 146–150 then carry the call out, until "every breathing thing" praises (150:6). In 11QPs-a each verse of the psalm is followed by a refrain, "Blessed be the LORD and blessed be his name for ever and ever", and after the last line the scribe wrote "This is for a memorial" (zot lezikkaron).

a: Praise the LORD!
p: Hallelu-yah, "Praise Yah!", begins and ends each of Psalms 146–150. The Plain renders it "Praise the LORD!".
b: Hallelu is the command "praise!" addressed to a group, and Yah is the short form of God's name (68:4; 118:5; Exodus 15:2). Together they make the word that English keeps as "Hallelujah" (from Hebrew) or "Alleluia" (from Greek and Latin). The site's Plain renders it "Praise the LORD!" everywhere (see 104:35, its first use). Psalms 146–150 form the Psalter's final "Hallel": each one opens and closes with it, so the book ends in ten hallelujahs. In the Greek, Allēlouia stands as a title above each psalm instead of at its end, and Greek copies add "Of Haggai and Zechariah" above 146, 147 (both halves) and 148. Revelation 19:1–6 has the only New Testament uses, in heaven's song at the fall of Babylon.

a: Do not rely on nobles
p: Princes die like everyone else, and their plans die with them. Trust belongs to God alone.
b: The warning echoes 118:8–9 (better to take shelter in the LORD than to trust in nobles) and Isaiah 2:22. It suited Israel after the exile, which lived under Persian, Greek and local rulers, none of whom could be counted on (compare Jeremiah 17:5–8). "A son of man" (ben adam) means simply a human being. "No rescue in him" can mean he cannot save others, or cannot save even himself, since he dies (146:4).

a: His breath leaves, he goes back to his ground
p: Ruach, breath or spirit, leaves the body, and the human (adam) returns to the ground (adamah), as Genesis 3:19 says.
b: The play on adam and adamah, human and ground, comes from Genesis 2:7 and 3:19: the LORD God shaped the man "from dust of the ground", and he will "go back to the ground". When God takes away breath, creatures die and return to their dust (104:29; Ecclesiastes 12:7; Job 34:14–15). "His schemes" ('eshtonotav) is a rare word, found only here, for plans or thoughts.
orig: תֵּצֵא רוּחוֹ יָשֻׁב לְאַדְמָתוֹ (tetse rucho yashuv le'admato)

a: maker of heaven and earth
t: Maker of heaven, earth and sea
p: The line repeats Exodus 20:11. The apostles pray it in Acts 4:24 and preach it in Acts 14:15.
b: The words follow the Sabbath commandment: "the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them" (Exodus 20:11). The early church prays them when threatened (Acts 4:24), Paul and Barnabas preach them to pagans at Lystra (Acts 14:15), and an angel in Revelation proclaims them to every nation (Revelation 14:7). "Maker of heaven and earth" is the same Hebrew phrase as in 115:15, 121:2, 124:8 and 134:3. The point here: a prince's breath stops (146:4), but the maker of everything "keeps faith for all time".

a: The LORD unties the prisoners.
p: Jewish morning prayers bless God "who frees the captives" and "who opens the eyes of the blind", words from 146:7–8.
b: The list of the LORD's deeds in 146:7–9 entered daily Jewish prayer. The morning blessings (birkhot hashachar) praise God "who opens the eyes of the blind" (poqeach 'ivrim), "who frees the captives" (matir 'asurim) and "who straightens those who are bent" (zoqef kefufim, compare 145:14), and the second of the Eighteen Benedictions (the Amidah) praises God who "sets the captives free". Christians hear the same list in Jesus' reading of Isaiah 61 at Nazareth (Luke 4:18) and in his answer to John the Baptist: the blind see, the poor hear good news (Matthew 11:5).

a: The LORD keeps watch over foreigners
p: The three most exposed people in Israel are under the LORD's own guard.
b: The foreigner who lives among Israel (ger), the orphan and the widow had no family land or male protector, and the law names them again and again (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17–21; Exodus 22:21–24). Deuteronomy says of the LORD: "He sees that the orphan and the widow get justice. He loves the foreigner" (Deuteronomy 10:18). The psalm calls him their guard and the one who helps them back up (ye'oded, the verb of 147:6). James calls care for orphans and widows pure religion (James 1:27).

a: The LORD will be king forever
p: The closing line echoes the Song of the Sea, and it is the last line of the Kedushah in Jewish prayer.
b: Moses' song at the sea ends "The LORD will be king forever and ever" (Exodus 15:18). This verse takes up the same verb, and adds "your God, Zion". In the synagogue it closes the Kedushah, the prayer of "Holy, holy, holy" (Isaiah 6:3) said during the repetition of the Amidah: "The LORD will be king forever, your God, Zion, for all generations. Praise the LORD!"

a: Praise the LORD!
p: The Hebrew counts Psalm 147 as one psalm. The Greek and Latin split it at 147:12, as their Psalms 146 and 147.
b: In Hebrew Bibles Psalm 147 runs 20 verses. The Greek, followed by the Latin Vulgate and the Catholic and Orthodox liturgies, divides it into two psalms: Psalm 146 (= 147:1–11) and Psalm 147 (= 147:12–20), each with its own "Hallelujah" heading. That is how the Greek numbering, one behind the Hebrew since Psalm 10, catches up: from Psalm 148 on the two systems agree again. The second half is the famous Lauda Jerusalem of Latin Vespers, set by Monteverdi (1610) and many others.

a: The LORD builds Jerusalem
p: Rebuilding Jerusalem and gathering Israel's outcasts point to the return from exile in the 500s and 400s BC.
b: "He gathers Israel's scattered outcasts" uses the phrase of Isaiah 56:8 (nidche Yisra'el; compare Isaiah 11:12). Building Jerusalem, strengthening the bars of its gates (147:13) and peace on its borders (147:14) suit the time of Nehemiah, when the walls were rebuilt and dedicated with songs and lyres (Nehemiah 12:27–43). Most scholars date the psalm after the exile; the Greek title naming Haggai and Zechariah, prophets of the rebuilt temple (Ezra 5:1), reflects the same reading.

a: He is the healer of those whose hearts are broken
p: The God who counts the stars (147:4) also bandages broken hearts. Isaiah 61:1 uses the same words.
b: "To bind up the broken of heart" is part of the mission of the anointed one in Isaiah 61:1, the passage Jesus reads in Nazareth (Luke 4:18). The psalm sets this beside the stars (147:4) on purpose: the God of the universe is not too great to tend a wound. "Broken-hearted" is in 34:18 too.

a: he calls each of them by a name
p: To name is to rule. Other peoples worshiped the stars; here they are counted and named by their maker.
b: Abraham could not count the stars (Genesis 15:5); God counts them and names them all (Isaiah 40:26). In Babylon the stars were gods, and their names were the names of gods; in Israel's faith they are creatures that answer when called (Isaiah 40:26; Baruch 3:34–35 has the stars answering "Here we are!"). The singer draws comfort from this: the God who knows every star knows every exile (Isaiah 40:27).

a: and the raven's chicks what they cry out for
p: The young ravens crying for food appear in Job 38:41, and Jesus points to the ravens in Luke 12:24.
b: In God's speech to Job the LORD asks who prepares the raven's food "when its chicks call to God for help" (Job 38:41). Jesus tells his disciples to consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, and God feeds them (Luke 12:24). The raven was an unclean bird (Leviticus 11:15), which makes God's care for it more striking. The rabbis told that the raven neglects its own chicks, so God feeds them himself (Rashi). The Greek adds a line to 147:8 from 104:14 (see the variant there).

a: The horse's might is not what he enjoys
p: God is not impressed by cavalry or fast runners, but by those who fear him and hope in his loyal love.
b: Horses and chariots were the tanks of the ancient world, and kings were warned not to build up horses (Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1; compare Psalm 20:7). "The legs of a man" are the strong thighs of a soldier or a runner (2 Samuel 2:18). What pleases God is fear and hope (147:11), the same contrast as 33:16–18.

a: Jerusalem, lift up the LORD's praise
p: Here the Greek and Latin begin a new psalm, their 147. It became a favorite psalm of Latin Vespers.
b: In the Greek this verse begins Psalm 147 with the heading "Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah". In the Latin Vulgate it is Lauda Jerusalem Dominum, lauda Deum tuum Sion, sung at Vespers on feasts of Mary and of virgin saints and set by composers such as Monteverdi (1610) and Vivaldi. Jewish prayer keeps the whole of Psalm 147 together in the daily morning psalms (see 145:0 and 150:6). The verb shabbechi, "lift up praise", is a word of later Hebrew and Aramaic, another sign of a date after the exile.

a: he feeds you full with the best of the wheat
p: "The fat of the wheat" is the finest grain. The same promise closes 81:16 and Deuteronomy 32:14.
b: "Best" renders chelev, "fat", the richest part. Israel is fed "the best of the wheat" in 81:16 and Deuteronomy 32:14. Peace on the borders and full storehouses were the signs of the covenant blessing (Leviticus 26:4–6). "He sets peace as your border" could also be read "he makes your territory peace".

a: his word comes running, fast
p: God's word is pictured as a runner who carries his orders to the earth: snow, frost, ice, then thaw.
b: In 147:15–18 God's "saying" and "word" act like messengers sent out to do his will (compare 107:20; Isaiah 55:10–11). The same word that brings winter brings the thaw (147:18). Then in 147:19 the psalm turns to the word God speaks to Israel: his rules and rulings. The pairing of the word in nature and the word in the law is also the shape of Psalm 19. Wisdom 18:15 pictures God's word leaping down from heaven like a warrior; John's Gospel calls the Son the Word (John 1:1–3).

a: He flings his ice like bits of bread
p: Pittim are morsels or crumbs. The picture is of hail thrown down like bits of bread.
b: Qerach is ice or hail, and pittim morsels, bits broken from bread (Genesis 18:5 uses the singular pat). Hail falling like scattered crumbs is a homely picture from the Jerusalem hills, where snow and hail fall most winters. The Greek has "crystal like morsels". A midrash reported by Rashi says God sends the cold in proportion to each person's clothing, sparing the poor.

a: his rules and his rulings to Israel
t: God's law given to Israel alone
p: The psalm ends with Israel's special gift: God has given his rules and rulings to Israel, as to no other nation.
b: "Rules and rulings" (chuqqim umishpatim) is the phrase of Deuteronomy for the whole covenant law (Deuteronomy 4:1, 5). Moses asked what great nation has rules and rulings as just as this whole law (Deuteronomy 4:8). The psalm sees this as Israel's greatest privilege: God shapes the weather for all, but he speaks his law to Jacob. Paul lists the same privilege: to Israel belong the covenants and the giving of the law (Romans 3:2; 9:4). Jewish readers have read the verse as the basis of Israel's calling to keep the Torah; many Christian readers, as the advantage Israel had in receiving God's word first.

a: Praise the LORD from the heavens
p: Psalm 148 calls on sun, sea monsters, hail and hills to praise. Are they really praising, or is this poetry?
b: The psalm moves down from the highest heavens (148:1–6) to the earth and its depths (148:7–12), the same order as Genesis 1: heavens, waters, lights, sea creatures, land animals, then humans. How can hail praise? Many readers say creation praises by being what it is and doing God's word (148:8; compare 19:1–4). Others, including many church fathers and Jewish mystics, hold that every creature has its own song (the later Jewish text Pereq Shirah assigns a verse to each creature). Modern readers have used the psalm for the care of creation: if everything praises God, nothing is only raw material.

a: praise him, all you his armies
p: Tseva'ot, "armies", are the hosts of heaven: angels, or the stars, as in the title "LORD of Armies".
b: The "armies" (tseva'av) of God are the heavenly hosts, whether angels (1 Kings 22:19) or the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 40:26). This is the word in the title "the LORD of Armies" (see 24:10). The plural "all his armies" is also in 103:21. The Greek has "all his powers" (dynameis).

a: and you waters over the heavens
p: The ancient picture of the world had waters above the sky's dome. The psalm calls on them too.
b: Genesis 1:7 says God divided "the waters under the dome from the waters above the dome", the waters that fall as rain when the "windows of the heavens" open (Genesis 7:11). "The heavens of the heavens" means the highest heavens (1 Kings 8:27; Deuteronomy 10:14). Readers differ over how to take this picture today: as the ancient description of the sky that Scripture uses without teaching it, as poetic language for clouds, or (in some creationist writing) as a real canopy of water. The psalm's point is only that nothing is too high to praise God.

a: he set a rule, and it will not be broken
p: Choq natan velo ya'avor can mean "a rule that will not pass away" or "a boundary none will cross".
b: Choq is a fixed rule or limit. God has set limits for the sea (Jeremiah 5:22; Job 38:10–11; Proverbs 8:29) and rules for the sun, moon and stars (Jeremiah 31:35–36; 33:25). The last words can be read "and it will not pass away" (the rule lasts) or "and they will not go beyond it" (none oversteps the limit). Rashi takes it of the decree that sun serves by day and moon by night. Jeremiah uses these fixed rules as proof that God will keep his covenant with Israel (Jeremiah 31:35–37).

a: you sea monsters and every ocean deep
p: The tanninim, monsters of the deep, were symbols of chaos in Canaanite myth. Here they join the choir.
b: Tanninim are the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21, and elsewhere the dragon of chaos that God defeats (74:13; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9). In Canaanite poems from Ugarit, Tunnan is a sea monster defeated by Baal and Anat. In this psalm, as in Genesis 1, the monsters are not God's rivals but his creatures, called with the ocean depths to praise him. The honest verdict: the Bible shares the old picture of sea monsters but denies them any power against God.

a: the storm wind that carries out his word
p: Fire, hail, snow and storm all do what God says. Jesus calms the storm with a word.
b: Hail and fire fell on Egypt at God's word (Exodus 9:23–24); the storm wind obeys him (107:25; 147:18), and the fiery messengers of 104:4 serve him. "Haze" renders qitor, smoke or thick fog (compare Genesis 19:28). In the Gospels the wind and the sea obey Jesus (Mark 4:41), which the disciples take as a sign of who he is.

a: kings of the earth and every people
p: Kings, officials and judges are called to praise the same God as young men and old women.
b: The list of humans runs from the top (kings, officials, judges) to everyone (young men and young women, old and young, 148:12). No rank, sex or age is left out. Kings who once plotted against the LORD (2:2, 10) are now summoned to praise him; compare 102:15 and 138:4. Revelation sees the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24).

a: He has lifted up a horn for his people
p: A horn is a sign of strength. "Lifting a horn" means giving victory, and later readers saw a king or Messiah.
b: A wild ox lifting its horns is a picture of strength and victory (75:10; 92:10; 1 Samuel 2:1, 10). God has "lifted up a horn" for Israel, made it strong again after its humiliation. Some read the horn as a king (132:17, "a horn for David"; 1 Samuel 2:10, "raise high his anointed one's horn"), and Zechariah's song in Luke takes up the image: "In the house of David his servant / he has raised up for us a horn of salvation" (Luke 1:69). "A people near to him" recalls Deuteronomy 4:7. In Vaticanus the line "a praise for all his loyal ones" is missing; the Gallican Latin has it.

a: his praise in the gathering of his loyal ones
p: Chasidim, "loyal ones", are those faithful to God's hesed. The word later named Jewish groups of strict piety.
b: Chasidim comes from hesed, loyal love: they are the people bound to God in covenant loyalty (145:10; 148:14; 149:5, 9). The word became the name of the "Hasideans" who supported the Maccabees in the 160s BC (1 Maccabees 2:42), and much later of the Hasidic movement of eighteenth-century Eastern Europe. Some scholars date Psalm 149 to the Maccabean wars because of its sword (149:6); most think it older.

a: Let them praise his name in the dance
p: Dance belonged to Israel's worship: Miriam at the sea, David before the ark, girls at the festivals.
b: Machol is a round dance. Miriam led the women with hand drums and dancing after the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:20), David danced before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14–16), and the girls of Shiloh danced at the yearly feast (Judges 21:21). At the Feast of Booths, the Mishnah says, pious men danced with torches in the temple courts (Mishnah Sukkah 5:4). Psalm 150:4 calls for dance again. Whether dance belongs in Christian worship is debated (see the traditions card on 2 Samuel 6).

a: let them ring out with joy upon their beds
p: On their beds may mean at night, lying down, or on the couches of a festival meal, or bowed on prayer mats.
b: Al mishkevotam, "on their beds", is unexpected in a psalm of victory. Some read it of praying at night (4:4; 63:6), others of the couches on which people reclined at feasts, or of the mats on which worshipers bowed. The Midrash on Psalms takes it of the righteous at rest on the couches prepared for them in the Garden of Eden (citing Isaiah 57:2). Hosea 7:14 condemns those who wail on their beds instead of crying to God; here the loyal shout for joy.

a: and a double-edged sword in their hand
p: Lofty praise in the throat, a two-edged sword in the hand: holy war, final judgment, or the sword of the word?
b: Readers have taken the sword in very different ways. (1) Literally: Israel's army praises God as it goes out against its oppressors, as Jehoshaphat's singers went before the army (2 Chronicles 20:21–22) and as Nehemiah's builders worked with a sword at their side (Nehemiah 4:17–18). (2) As the end-time judgment, carried out at God's command and "written" in advance (149:9; compare Daniel 7:22; 1 Corinthians 6:2). (3) Figuratively: the praises themselves are the sword, as Rashi reads it, and Christians link the two-edged sword to God's word (Hebrews 4:12; Ephesians 6:17; Revelation 1:16). Delitzsch reports that this psalm was used to stir up religious wars, by Caspar Schoppe for the Catholic side in the Thirty Years' War and by Thomas Müntzer in the Peasants' War, a warning of what a literal reading can do.
r: 2 Chronicles 20:21–22; Nehemiah 4:17–18; Hebrews 4:12; Ephesians 6:17; Revelation 1:16; Revelation 19:15

a: to bring vengeance on the nations
p: The psalm gives the loyal a part in God's vengeance. Jewish and Christian readers both say vengeance belongs to God.
b: The "vengeance" (neqamah) is not private revenge but the punishment of oppressors by the rightful judge (Deuteronomy 32:35, 43). The Midrash on Psalms stresses that vengeance is God's, and that it falls on the kings who attacked Israel (149:8), not on all people. Christian readers point to Romans 12:19 ("make room for the anger") and read the psalm of the last judgment, or of the spiritual struggle against evil.

a: the sentence that is written
p: The "written" sentence may be in the law, in the prophets, or in God's book of judgment.
b: Mishpat katuv, "a written judgment", may point to the law's commands against Israel's enemies (Deuteronomy 7:1–2; 25:19), to the prophets' oracles against the nations, or to the decrees written in heaven (Isaiah 65:6; Daniel 7:10). Rashi refers it to Ezekiel 25:14, "I will set my vengeance on Edom by the hand of my people Israel", and explains that David prophesied of the end of days. The Great Psalms Scroll adds after "his loyal ones" the words "to the children of Israel, his holy people".

a: Praise God in his holy place
t: In his holy place, or among his holy ones?
p: Qodesh can mean the sanctuary or holiness. The Greek read "among his holy ones", the saints or angels.
b: Beqodsho may mean "in his sanctuary", the temple on earth, matched by "the dome of his power", the sky above it, so that earth and heaven praise together. The Greek has en tois hagiois autou, "in his holy places" or "among his holy ones", and the Latin in sanctis eius, which church tradition read as "in his saints". Note that here God is called El, the ancient name for God, not the divine name.

a: praise him in the dome of his power
p: Raqia', the "dome" or "firmament" of Genesis 1, is the sky. Its only use in the Psalms besides 19:1.
b: Raqia' is the word of Genesis 1:6–8 for the solid-looking sky that God spread out, the site's "dome" (KJV "firmament", from the Latin firmamentum and the Greek stereōma, "something made firm"). Psalm 19:1 says it reports the work of God's hands. Here it is "the dome of his power", the sky as the sign of his strength.

a: Praise him with a blast on the ram's horn
p: Ram's horn, harp, lyre, drum, strings, pipe and two kinds of cymbals: the whole temple orchestra and more.
b: The shofar (ram's horn) was blown by priests for signals and feasts (81:3; Leviticus 25:9). The nevel and kinnor, harp and lyre, were the Levites' stringed instruments (1 Chronicles 15:16; 25:1). The tof was a frame drum, played by women in dances (Exodus 15:20). Minnim means "strings", and the 'ugav, a reed pipe or flute, is the instrument of Jubal (Genesis 4:21). The tseltselim were bronze cymbals, the instrument of Asaph (1 Chronicles 16:5). Priests' horn, Levites' strings and the people's drums and dances are all called in at once. The Greek has "trumpet" for shofar and organon ("instrument") for 'ugav; Jerome's Latin organo is the word from which "organ" comes.

a: praise him with cymbals of the loud shout
p: Tseltsele shama' and tseltsele teru'ah: cymbals "of hearing" and cymbals "of shouting". Perhaps small and large.
b: The first pair are "cymbals of sound" or "of hearing", the second "cymbals of the shout", teru'ah being the war cry or the trumpet blast of the feasts (Numbers 10:5–9; Joshua 6:5). They may be two sizes of cymbal, the soft and the loud, or the same instrument played two ways.

a: Let every breathing thing praise Yah!
p: Kol hanneshamah, "all breath", means every living creature. The divine name here is the short form Yah.
b: Neshamah is the breath of life God blew into the first human (Genesis 2:7), and "everything with breath" can mean all living creatures (Genesis 7:22) or humans in particular (Joshua 10:40). The book that began with one happy person meditating on God's law (1:1–2) ends with every breathing thing praising. The verb is singular, "let all breath praise"; the Great Psalms Scroll has the plural "all breaths". The name is Yah, as in hallelu-yah, and the Plain keeps it here, as in 118:5. The Greek has "Let every breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah."
orig: כֹּל הַנְּשָׁמָה תְּהַלֵּל יָהּ (kol hanneshamah tehallel yah)

a: Praise the LORD!
p: Each of the five books ends with a doxology. Psalm 150 closes Book V and the whole book.
b: Book I ends with "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel" (41:13), Book II at 72:18–19, Book III at 89:52, and Book IV at 106:48. Book V has no single line of blessing; instead the whole of Psalm 150, perhaps all of 146–150, serves as its doxology and that of the entire Psalter. In Jewish morning prayer, 145–150 are said every day, and the Talmud's wish to be among "those who complete the Hallel every day" is understood of these psalms (Bavli Shabbat 118b, with Rashi). In the church, 148–150 were sung every morning at the end of Lauds, which takes its name from their Laudate, "Praise!", and they are the "Praises" of Orthodox Matins.
